title: Durable, high-bandwidth two-way neural interface

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a neural interface that can reliably read intended actions and return useful sensory information through neural stimulation over years of everyday use. Its outward channel would translate neural activity into communication or control of a physical or virtual hand. Its inward channel would provide sensory feedback that helps the user guide those actions. Durability means preserving safe, useful function through changing neural signals, repeated use and practical maintenance. High bandwidth means enough selective, usable information to support the intended tasks; electrode count or raw data rate alone would not establish that capability. This is a synthesis of the proposed concept, not an achieved result.

The supplied study demonstrates an important part of this architecture: an implanted intracortical brain–computer interface decoded attempted speech and right-hand motor imagery into speech output, cursor movement and mouse clicks during extended home use. It did not demonstrate neural sensory stimulation. Combining multiple decoded outputs therefore establishes multimodal control, but does not by itself establish a two-way neural interface.

significance.text: Reliable everyday decoding can give people with severe paralysis and speech impairment useful ways to communicate and operate digital tools. Card and colleagues provide a concrete basis for this significance: one participant used speech and cursor decoding at home without researcher supervision after care-partner setup. The advance matters because useful assistive function must survive daily use beyond scheduled laboratory sessions.

Conditional impact synthesis: adding durable neural sensory feedback and sufficiently capable hand control could extend communication and digital access into sustained closed-loop interaction. Feedback that reliably informs the user about the controlled hand could improve manipulation and reduce the effort needed to monitor actions. If these benefits generalized across many users, the result could be a transformative assistive capability. Reduced dependence on caregivers or broader participation in work and daily activities would remain downstream possibilities requiring direct evaluation.

Limits of the proposed impact: this would be a task-specific interface to selected neural signals and stimulation targets, not evidence of arbitrary thought reading or a treatment for every neurological condition. Useful artificial sensation would also not automatically reproduce natural sensation in its full richness. Two-dimensional cursor control cannot be treated as evidence of dexterous hand restoration, and success in one participant cannot establish broad clinical applicability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing integrated capability is sustained, practical two-way function: selective neural recording, stable decoding, useful control and beneficial neural sensory stimulation working together over long periods. The supplied study identifies chronic neural signal variability and the need for recording sensors and decoding performance to remain stable. Calibration, wired access, setup and portability also constrain the demonstrated recording-based system. These are concrete obstacles to making everyday operation dependable and convenient.

Engineering synthesis: the sensory channel would need stimulation that conveys interpretable, task-relevant information with adequate selectivity, while preserving useful recording and control. The system would need to maintain that relationship as signals and user strategies change. Electrode design, recording and stimulation electronics, signal processing, decoding, power and system integration must jointly support this goal. More channels would be valuable only insofar as they improve reliable functional information and user benefit.

Additional barriers retained from the proposed concept include tissue response, access to suitable neural populations, safe long-term stimulation and practical power provision. Their importance and tractability for a particular architecture cannot be assessed from the supplied study alone. Its recording and decoding results do not establish chronic stimulation safety, quantify tissue-response limits or resolve the full power problem. The authors also did not systematically assess user fatigue or long-term device wear, limiting what sustained decoding performance can establish about overall durability.

current_state.text: In “Long-term independent use of an intracortical brain–computer interface for speech and cursor control,” reported on 15 June 2026, Nicholas S. Card and colleagues described one man with paralysis and severe dysarthria due to ALS using the system at home nearly every day for 19 months. He accumulated more than 3,800 hours of independent use. Independence here meant operation without researcher supervision; trained care partners assisted with putting on and removing hardware and initializing software. It did not mean assistance-free setup or removal.

In prompted speech-copy benchmarks, silent speech averaged 49.7 words per minute with reported word accuracy of 96.5%. Vocalized speech averaged 30.6 words per minute with accuracy exceeding 99%. These figures describe the reported benchmark conditions and should not be presented as measured accuracy during unrestricted everyday conversation. The distinction preserves the strength of the demonstrated performance without extending it to an unevaluated setting.

Two additional decoders translated right-hand motor imagery into two-dimensional cursor control and discrete mouse clicks. A gaze-controlled toggle activated these decoders, and gaze tracking assisted interface use. The study therefore demonstrated practical speech and cursor control through an interface combining neural decoding with other interaction support. It did not demonstrate dexterous physical-hand control or a neural sensory return channel.

The demonstrated duration and extensive home use are substantial evidence of sustained assistive decoding in this participant. Generalizability to other people, implant sites, intracortical electrode types and neurological conditions remained unknown. Continued decoding performance also cannot substitute for the systematic assessments of fatigue and long-term device wear that the study did not perform. These limits leave broader durability and two-way restoration unresolved; they do not negate the reported home-use result.

Evidence scope: according to the supplied research and validated review, the accessible article text was inspected, including full main text, methods and references, with no reported extraction truncation. The publisher PDF failed to open, so the numerical account here rests on the reviewed article text rather than a separate PDF or figure inspection. The supplied search record was empty, leaving field-wide freshness unassessed, including the review's referenced 1 November 2026 assessment date. This record supports the dated June 2026 result but cannot establish whether subsequent work achieved additional capabilities.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: an appropriately designed clinical program should show years of everyday use in a diverse cohort, combining communication with control of a physical or virtual hand and an explicit neural sensory stimulation channel. Feedback should measurably improve prespecified task performance or another meaningful functional outcome compared with an appropriate control condition. The duration, cohort composition and required improvement would be proposed evaluation choices, not established standards supplied by the article.
completion_criteria.label: Years of bidirectional everyday use with feedback improving functional outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed operational definitions: independence should specify permitted care-partner help, including setup, removal, software initialization, calibration and troubleshooting. Trials should distinguish researcher-free operation from assistance-free use and report how much help is required in practice. Functional endpoints should separate prompted benchmarks from spontaneous communication and everyday control, and should account for supporting inputs such as gaze tracking.
completion_criteria.label: Report practical assistance requirements and distinguish everyday functional endpoints

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and safety assessment: prespecify long-term safety, functional benefit, user control, fatigue, maintenance burden and device-wear outcomes. Track performance drift, calibration needs, interruptions, repairs and stimulation tolerability alongside successful task use. Users should be able to initiate and stop operation and retain meaningful control over outputs. Practical success should include a maintenance and support burden compatible with the intended home setting.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate long-term safety, user control and manageable home maintenance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility boundary: demonstrate repeatable benefit across participants, repeated sessions and relevant everyday environments, with sufficiently documented hardware, decoding, stimulation and assistance procedures to support independent evaluation. Report the tested conditions and failures explicitly. A finite clinical program could establish convincing breadth within those boundaries; it could not establish literal universality across people, neural targets, tasks or diseases.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce benefits across participants, sessions and environments within documented limits

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison synthesis: ELE-08, “Manufacturable ultra-low-voltage switching for general-purpose electronics,” and ELE-11, “Integrated photonic-electronic computing with broad system advantage,” concern potential enabling electronics and computation. Improvements in those areas could help neural-interface processing or power budgets, but would not establish safe chronic recording, interpretable sensory stimulation or clinical benefit. ELE-06 is defined by durable two-way function at the neural and user interface.

Roster comparison synthesis: ELE-07, “Infrastructure-scale wireless electrical power delivery,” and ELE-10, “Broadly deployable, maintenance-free ambient-powered sensing,” overlap with questions of power provision, sensing and maintenance. Their scales and operating environments differ from implanted neural systems. Neither infrastructure-scale wireless power nor ambient-powered sensing would by itself resolve the selectivity, chronic operation and functional-feedback requirements of ELE-06.

Roster comparison synthesis: ELE-01, “Practical ambient-temperature superconducting conductors,” ELE-05, “Cheap, scalable storage for weeks to seasons of electrical supply,” and ELE-09, “Resilient, self-restoring power networks,” address electrical conduction, energy supply and grid reliability. Those advances could contribute to the wider infrastructure supporting assistive technologies, but their completion would not demonstrate a neural interface. ELE-06 has distinct biological, clinical and interaction requirements.

Roster comparison synthesis: ELE-02, “Fault-tolerant quantum computer with useful, scalable logical computation,” ELE-03, “A long-distance quantum repeater network,” and ELE-04, “Practical, energy-recovering reversible computing,” address different computation or communication capabilities. The supplied material establishes no requirement that ELE-06 depend on these breakthroughs. Neural decoding and sensory stimulation should be evaluated through their own functional and clinical evidence, without importing claims of quantum or reversible-computing advantage.

Disciplinary synthesis: ELE-06 also overlaps neuroscience, clinical medicine, rehabilitation and robotics. Electrical engineering supplies electrodes, electronics, signal processing, power and integration; clinical and behavioral evaluation must establish safety and useful function. These relationships explain its interdisciplinary character while preserving its identity as a durable, high-bandwidth two-way neural interface.

unresolved_issues: The supplied material does not establish the field's latest status or whether later studies demonstrated additional two-way capabilities.
The magnitude and tractability of tissue response, power, neural-population access and chronic selective-stimulation constraints require additional evidence.
The study does not establish generalizability across participants, implant sites, electrode types or neurological conditions.
Long-term fatigue, device wear and the safety and utility of chronic neural sensory stimulation remain insufficiently evaluated in the supplied evidence.
Trial duration, cohort diversity, permitted assistance, functional success thresholds and acceptable maintenance burden remain to be operationally defined.
The functional information rate and selectivity needed to justify high bandwidth depend on the intended tasks and remain unspecified.
The publisher PDF was inaccessible in the supplied research; the record relies on the article text described in the validated review.

brief.title: A lasting brain link for speech, movement and touch
possible: People with severe paralysis could communicate and control a physical or virtual hand through their intended actions, while receiving useful sensations through electrical brain stimulation. They could rely on this link for years of everyday use.
why: Reliable communication and computer access would help people with severe paralysis and speech impairment stay connected and use digital tools at home. Sensations from a controlled hand could make handling objects easier and reduce the effort of watching every movement.

sources.showed: A man with paralysis used an implanted brain interface for speech and cursor control at home for 19 months. Care partners helped with setup and removal; researchers did not supervise daily use.
sources.quote: The participant also used the speech BCI as keyboard input and the cursor BCI as mouse input to control his personal computer, enabling him to send text messages and emails and to browse the internet.
sources.cited_for: Brain signals can support sustained communication and computer use at home.
sources.not_established: The study did not demonstrate sensory feedback through brain stimulation or skilled hand control.

sources.showed: A participant with paralysis controlled a robotic arm using brain signals. Adding touch sensations through electrical brain stimulation halved task completion times.
sources.quote: Faster times were primarily due to less time spent attempting to grasp objects
sources.cited_for: Touch feedback through brain stimulation can improve robotic arm control.
sources.not_established: The result does not establish years of everyday use or benefits across users.

sources.showed: Electrical brain stimulation continued to evoke hand sensations for up to 10 years. Some electrodes lost this ability, but no serious adverse events were reported.
sources.quote: ICMS consistently evoked sensations localized to the hand.
sources.cited_for: Electrical brain stimulation can preserve useful touch sensations over long periods.
sources.not_established: This small trial does not establish the safety and usefulness of a complete system during everyday home use.

shown: Card and colleagues demonstrated speech and cursor control during 19 months of home use by a man with paralysis. He operated without researcher supervision after care-partner setup, with gaze tracking also helping him use the system.

Flesher and colleagues showed that artificial touch improved robotic arm control in a participant with paralysis. Separately, Greenspon and colleagues found that brain stimulation could still evoke hand sensations after a decade.
missing: A complete system has yet to combine communication, hand control and beneficial brain-delivered sensations over years of everyday use.
Safe, useful operation must withstand changing brain signals, repeated stimulation and device wear with manageable setup, power and maintenance.
The combined benefits have yet to be reproduced across diverse users and everyday settings.

milestones.label: Years of everyday control with useful sensory feedback
milestones.explanation: A diverse group would need years of everyday communication and physical or virtual hand control, with brain stimulation improving meaningful outcomes against a comparison condition. This would establish lasting practical benefit.

milestones.label: Clear measures of assistance and everyday performance
milestones.explanation: Trials would need to report setup and ongoing help, distinguish researcher-free from assistance-free use, and separate prompted tests from everyday performance, including gaze support. This would clarify practical independence.

milestones.label: Lasting safety, user control and manageable maintenance
milestones.explanation: Long-term tests would need to track safety, benefit, fatigue, wear, performance changes and upkeep while users retain control, including starting and stopping. This would establish whether home use remains safe and manageable.

milestones.label: Repeatable benefits across users and everyday settings
milestones.explanation: Benefits would need to recur across participants, sessions and everyday settings, with procedures and failures documented for independent evaluation. This would establish where the system reliably works.

uncertain: How much useful information and sensory detail would different everyday tasks require?
How would tissue responses, power needs and long-term stimulation limit performance?
What duration, user diversity, improvement and maintenance burden would count as success?

page.title: Bidirectional intracortical brain–computer interfaces for home use
page.definition: An implanted brain–computer interface decodes intended actions and returns task-relevant sensations through electrical stimulation of the brain. Recording, control and sensory feedback remain safe and effective together over years of home use.

goal.need: Sensory feedback addresses a measured limitation of brain-controlled manipulation: in one participant with tetraplegia, adding brain-delivered touch reduced median robotic-arm task time by 51.2%. Separately, one man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis accumulated more than 3,800 hours of speech-and-cursor BCI use over 19 months at home. Together these results motivate combining sensory benefit with sustained access outside laboratory sessions.

figures.caption: Robotic-arm performance with and without intracortical tactile feedback.
figures.note: One participant with tetraplegia; modified Action Research Arm Test; published on 21 May 2021.

completion.title: FDA grants premarket approval for a bidirectional intracortical BCI for multi-year home use.
completion.criterion: FDA grants premarket approval for an intracortical BCI whose approved intended use includes decoded action control and task-relevant sensory feedback delivered through brain stimulation during home use over a specified multi-year implanted service life. The approval must cover the integrated system and these uses. Device-specific functional performance, adverse events, durability and assistance requirements must support FDA's safety-and-effectiveness determination.
completion.set_by: FDA, Premarket Approval framework, applied to the integrated sensorimotor home-use indication specified here.
completion.threshold_quote: the PMA contains sufficient valid scientific evidence to assure that the device is safe and effective for its intended use(s).
completion.basis: FDA supplies an external, intended-use-specific safety-and-effectiveness decision. Its implanted-BCI guidance addresses recording, stimulation, home operation and long-term reliability. Approval must encompass both neural directions and the claimed duration. This framework supplies no universal information-rate or multi-year lifetime threshold; those remain specific to the device and intended use.

milestones.title: An implanted BCI demonstrates nonclinical safety sufficient to support human implantation.
milestones.criterion: Bench testing and justified animal studies establish preliminary safety for the proposed clinical exposure. For a recording-and-stimulation BCI, FDA identifies stimulation-evoked responses, acute and chronic recording quality, surrounding-tissue histopathology and examination of explanted components. Animal numbers and exposure duration depend on device risks; FDA publishes no universal numerical pass threshold.
milestones.set_by: FDA, implanted-BCI guidance, sections III(N) and III(O); recommendations are nonbinding and device-specific.

milestones.title: FDA authorizes a clinical study of an implanted recording-and-stimulation BCI.
milestones.criterion: FDA approves an Investigational Device Exemption for the proposed significant-risk clinical investigation after assessing preliminary safety and the study's benefit–risk balance. Authorization permits the specified clinical study; it does not authorize marketing. The subsequent human studies cited below establish that investigational cortical recording-and-stimulation systems have reached this stage.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Regulatory Overview for Neurological Devices, Investigational Device Exemptions section.
milestones.threshold_quote: The FDA will generally approve the study if the potential benefits justify the risks, and if remaining risks have been appropriately minimized.

milestones.title: An implanted BCI demonstrates action control and neural sensory feedback in people.
milestones.criterion: An early feasibility investigation establishes initial clinical safety and device functionality for the intended recording-and-stimulation use. FDA describes such studies as generally involving fewer than 10 initial subjects, rather than prescribing a success sample size. Flesher and colleagues demonstrated brain-controlled robotic manipulation with beneficial intracortical tactile feedback in one participant; the result was published on 21 May 2021.
milestones.set_by: FDA, early-feasibility guidance, section 3; applied to sensorimotor BCI functionality.
milestones.threshold_quote: initial clinical safety and device functionality

milestones.title: A cortical recording-and-stimulation implant avoids safety-driven removal for 12 months.
milestones.criterion: The implant is not removed for safety reasons during the 12-month post-implant evaluation. This is the published safety endpoint for NCT01894802, not a claim of complete functional stability. Greenspon and colleagues reported stimulation outcomes in five participants on 15 July 2026, including hand sensations after 10 years in one participant. They reported 53 stimulation-related adverse events, consisting of persistent sensations, with no lasting effects.
milestones.set_by: NCT01894802 protocol, as reproduced in SCOPE's clinical-trials table dated 19 October 2015, page 6; the threshold appears in a table.

milestones.title: Intended users operate the final home BCI with acceptable risks from use errors.
milestones.criterion: Human-factors validation tests the final interface, all critical tasks and representative home conditions with intended users. FDA generally recommends at least 15 participants per distinct user population. Serious use errors must be reduced; persisting errors require evidence that further reduction is impractical and benefits outweigh residual risks. Card and colleagues' home decoding result supports feasibility, but includes care-partner setup and no neural sensory feedback; it does not establish this integrated validation.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Applying Human Factors and Usability Engineering to Medical Devices, sections 8, 8.1.1 and 8.1.7.
milestones.threshold_quote: without serious use errors or problems, for the intended uses and under the expected use conditions.

milestones.title: A pivotal study establishes the integrated BCI's safety and effectiveness for its intended home use.
milestones.criterion: A pivotal investigation provides definitive evidence of safety and effectiveness for the specified integrated home-use indication, using its prespecified success criteria and statistical analysis. FDA's implanted-BCI guidance recommends at least 1 year of long-term follow-up. Numerical functional targets, sample size and additional follow-up must come from the device's protocol; the guidance supplies no universal values. This is the clinical-evidence stage preceding a marketing decision.
milestones.set_by: FDA, early-feasibility guidance's definition of a pivotal study and implanted-BCI guidance, sections III(O)(c) and III(O)(e).
milestones.threshold_quote: collect definitive evidence of the safety and effectiveness of a device for a specified intended use

not_found: No universal clinical threshold for useful bidirectional information rate or multi-year implanted service life was found in the FDA guidance or DARPA and NIH programme documents searched.
No published pivotal protocol specifying numerical success criteria for the complete multi-year home sensorimotor capability was found.
ClinicalTrials.gov did not expose readable protocol text for NCT01894802; its historical safety endpoint was available in SCOPE's published table.
The Greenspon article's PMC full text was blocked by a browser check, and its publisher page returned HTTP 403.

results.finding: One participant used an intracortical speech and cursor BCI at home for 19 months.
results.detail: Care partners assisted with setup. The research system did not provide neural sensory feedback, and the study did not validate a final integrated home interface or assess critical use errors.
results.quote: With care partner assistance largely restricted to donning and doffing the hardware and initializing the software, a man with paralysis and severe dysarthria due to ALS used the system in his home nearly every day for 19 months, accumulating more than 3,800 h of independent use.

results.finding: One participant used a bidirectional BCI to control a robotic arm; median task time fell from 20.9 to 10.2 seconds with tactile feedback.
results.detail: Intracortical stimulation supplied tactile feedback during robotic manipulation. The single-subject result may not generalize to other participants.
results.quote: This enabled a person with tetraplegia to substantially improve performance with a robotic limb; trial times on a clinical upper-limb assessment were reduced by half, from a median time of 20.9 to 10.2 s.

results.finding: All 5 participants met the endpoint of no safety-driven explantation within 1 year.
results.detail: The study reported 53 stimulation-related adverse events, all persistent sensations, with no lasting effects.
results.quote: The primary outcome measure for the clinical trial is the safety of the participants, specifically that the device does not need to be explanted due to a safety concern within the first year of implantation. This criterion was met for all participants.

results.finding: FDA IDE G170010 authorized the BiCNS study of implanted recording and stimulation arrays; this report covers 1 participant.
results.detail: The reported experiments used recording for connection verification and safety monitoring, while stimulation elicited tactile sensations.
results.quote: This study was conducted under Investigational Device Exemption (IDE G170010) by the FDA for the purpose of evaluating bilateral sensory and motor capabilities of microelectrode array implants. The study protocol was approved by the FDA,

results.finding: In 3 participants with spinal cord injury, intracortical stimulation evoked tactile sensations.
results.detail: The study reports sensory feedback and tests localization using a bionic hand, but the provided text does not demonstrate participant-controlled action with that feedback or establish initial clinical safety for combined recording and stimulation.
results.quote: In all three participants, stimulation through electrodes in S1 evoked sensations experienced on the contralateral hand
